newsitem.title: INDIA: Bhutan economy well run, but needs fiscal caution.
newsitem.headline: Bhutan economy well run, but needs fiscal caution.

text.p: The remote Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan runs a sound economy, albeit dependent on foreign aid and budgetary support from neighboring India, but caution is needed over future budgets, the Asian Development Bank said in its annual report released on Thursday.
Recurrent expenditure will exceed domestic revenues this year for the first time since 1992, the ADB report said.
Growing health and education budgets and a 25 percent increase in civil servants' salaries are the main reason why Bhutan needs to keep a watch on fiscal balances, it said.
Bhutan will encounter difficulty squeezing more revenues from taxes and duties, it added.
"Over the medium term, the government will need to exercise great fiscal prudence, especially since the revenue base is both narrow and inelastic," the report said.
It described last year's fiscal policy as prudent and overall the ADB praised Bhutan's economic record.
"Careful macroeconomic management has resulted in sound fiscal and external balances and stable price conditions," it said.
In 1996 Bhutan ran a budget surplus of 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The commissioning of the Chukha hydroelectric plant and establishment of energy intensive industries, most government-owned, has led to an increase in manufacturing's share of GDP in the agricultural-based economy.
Real GDP grew 6.4 percent in 1996, reflecting higher cement production and output from a new ferro-alloy plant.
But because no big projects are scheduled to be completed before the new century GDP growth is expected to slow to five percent this year.
Monetary growth stayed around 30 percent in 1996, while inflation was estimated at nine percent, largely reflecting price movements in India -- the landlocked state's largest trading partner.
Inflows of foreign money, mainly concessional loans and grants, more than offset a 1996 current account deficit of $48 million, which was 14 percent of GDP.
The current account deficit was expected to balloon to 26 percent of GDP over this year and next, due to imports associated with projects under construction.
The inflows of foreign aid boosted gross foreign exchange reserves $25 milion to $145 million by the end of 1996, equivalent to more than 16 months of imports.
External debt was around 34 percent of GDP, and while the debt service ratio was around 23.5 percent in 1996 it was expected to stabilise at between 16-18 percent next year.
